source.title: Help Someone Who Is Struggling
source.attribution: A Reborn guide drawing on the National Institute of Mental Health, Mind, the NHS, the World Health Organization and NICE.
source.notes: Written by Reborn; no text copied. References: National Institute of Mental Health, 5 Action Steps to Help Someone Having Thoughts of Suicide, https://www.nimh.nih.gov/health/publications/5-action-steps-to-help-someone-having-thoughts-of-suicide; National Institute of Mental Health, Warning Signs of Suicide, https://www.nimh.nih.gov/health/publications/warning-signs-of-suicide; Mind, Supporting someone with a mental health problem, https://www.mind.org.uk/information-support/helping-someone-else/supporting-someone-with-a-mental-health-problem/; NHS, Help for suicidal thoughts, https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/feelings-symptoms-behaviours/behaviours/help-for-suicidal-thoughts/; World Health Organization, Suicide fact sheet, https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/suicide; NICE, Self-harm: assessment, management and preventing recurrence (NG225), https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng225

cards.title: You can make a real difference to someone who is struggling
cards.body:
When someone you care about is having a hard time, it is natural to worry about saying the wrong thing. This guide will help you feel more confident.

You will learn how to spot signs that someone may be struggling, how to start a conversation, and how to listen without rushing to fix things. You will learn what not to say, why asking directly about suicide is safe, how to help someone find professional support, and what to do in a crisis. Finally, you will look at supporting someone over time and looking after yourself.

You do not need to be an expert. If anyone is in immediate danger, contact local emergency services or a crisis line straight away.
cards.apply_it: Think of one person you are worried about, or might be one day, and keep them in mind as you read.

quiz.question: What does this guide say you need to help someone who is struggling?
options: A medical degree
Care, willingness to listen and some simple skills
Perfect words every time
A solution to all their problems
quiz.explanation: You do not need to be an expert. Caring, listening and knowing a few steps can make a real difference.

cards.title: You do not need the perfect words, just to show you care
cards.body:
Many people stay quiet because they fear they will say the wrong thing or make things worse. Mental health charities such as Mind stress that you do not need to be an expert or have all the answers.

What often helps most is simply showing that you have noticed and that you care. A short, warm message like I have been thinking about you, how are you really doing? can mean a lot.

Your role is to be a supportive friend, partner or family member, not a therapist. You can listen, offer kindness, and help them find professional support if they need it.

If you get something wrong, you can say sorry and try again.
cards.apply_it: Write a short, warm message you could send to someone you are worried about.

quiz.question: What is your main role when supporting someone?
options: Acting as their therapist
Fixing all of their problems
Showing you care, listening and helping them find support
Staying quiet in case you say the wrong thing
quiz.explanation: Your role is to be caring and supportive and to help them find professional help, not to be their therapist.

cards.title: Changes in behaviour can be a sign someone is struggling
cards.body:
People do not always say when they are finding things hard. Often, the first clues are changes in what they do.

You might notice someone withdrawing from friends or activities they used to enjoy, sleeping much more or less, eating differently, or seeming tired all the time. They may drink more, stop looking after themselves, take more time off work or school, or seem restless, irritable or tearful.

The key word is change. Everyone has off days, but a shift that lasts for weeks, or that seems out of character, is worth paying attention to.

Trust your instincts. If something feels wrong, it is okay to check in gently.
cards.apply_it: Think about whether anyone close to you has changed in a lasting way lately.

quiz.question: What is a key sign to look out for?
options: A lasting change in behaviour that seems out of character
Someone having one bad day
Someone being quiet by nature
Someone enjoying their hobbies
quiz.explanation: Lasting or out-of-character changes, like withdrawing or sleeping differently, are worth noticing and gently checking.

cards.title: What people say can hint at how they really feel
cards.body:
Sometimes people show how they feel through what they say, often in passing or as a joke.

Listen out for comments like I am so tired of everything, what is the point, I am a burden, nobody would notice if I was not here, or I cannot do this anymore. People may also talk about feeling trapped, hopeless, worthless or numb.

These comments are easy to brush off, especially if they are said with a laugh. But they can be a way of testing whether it is safe to talk.

If you hear something like this, it is a good moment to gently ask more. You might say, you said earlier that you feel like a burden. Can you tell me more about that?
cards.apply_it: If someone makes a worrying comment, gently ask them to tell you more about it.

quiz.question: How should you respond if a friend jokes that nobody would notice if they were gone?
options: Laugh along and change the subject
Tell them off for saying it
Ignore it, they were only joking
Gently ask them to tell you more about how they feel
quiz.explanation: Worrying comments, even as jokes, can be a way of testing the waters. Asking gently shows it is safe to talk.

cards.title: Know the warning signs that someone may be at risk of suicide
cards.body:
Organisations such as the US National Institute of Mental Health list warning signs that a person may be thinking about suicide.

These include talking about wanting to die or feeling hopeless, feeling trapped or in unbearable pain, talking about being a burden, withdrawing from others, giving away important belongings, saying goodbye to people, searching for ways to end their life, and big mood swings, including a sudden calm after a time of deep distress.

These signs do not always mean someone is about to act, and some people show no clear signs. But if you notice them, take them seriously and talk to the person. If you think they are in immediate danger, contact local emergency services straight away.
cards.apply_it: Read through the warning signs once more so you will recognise them if you see them.

quiz.question: Which of these is a recognised warning sign of suicide?
options: Planning a holiday with friends
Giving away important belongings and saying goodbye
Starting a new hobby
Complaining about the weather
quiz.explanation: Giving away belongings and saying goodbye are recognised warning signs. They should be taken seriously.

cards.title: Pick a calm, private moment to start the conversation
cards.body:
Where and when you talk can make a difference. Try to choose a time when you will not be rushed or interrupted, and a place where the person feels comfortable.

Many people find it easier to talk side by side rather than face to face. A walk, a drive or doing a task together, like washing up, can take the pressure off. Eye contact can feel intense when you are sharing something painful.

Avoid times when either of you is very tired, stressed or has been drinking.

If you cannot meet in person, a phone call or message is better than nothing. The most important thing is that they know you care and want to listen.
cards.apply_it: Suggest a walk or a coffee with the person you are worried about this week.

quiz.question: Why might talking side by side, such as on a walk, help?
options: It is quicker
It means you do not have to listen
It can feel less intense than direct eye contact
It stops the person talking
quiz.explanation: Side-by-side activities can make sharing feel less pressured than sitting face to face.

cards.title: Open the conversation gently and honestly
cards.body:
There is no perfect opening line, but simple and honest is usually best.

You could start by saying what you have noticed and that you care: I have noticed you have seemed quieter lately, and I wanted to check how you are doing. Or: You do not seem yourself recently. I am here if you want to talk.

Open questions, which cannot be answered with just yes or no, invite people to share more. How have things been for you lately? is better than Are you okay?

Asking twice can help too. Many of us say fine automatically. A gentle, are you sure? How are you really? shows you genuinely want to know.
cards.apply_it: Practise one opening line out loud, using what you have noticed and an open question.

quiz.question: Which is the best opening question?
options: How have things been for you lately?
You are fine, aren't you?
Why are you being so moody?
Did something bad happen or not?
quiz.explanation: Open questions invite people to talk. Closed or judging questions can make them shut down.

cards.title: If they say they are fine, leave the door open
cards.body:
Sometimes people are not ready to talk, even if they are struggling. They may feel embarrassed, worried about being a burden, or not yet sure what they feel.

If they say they are fine, do not push too hard. Pushing can make people feel cornered. Instead, let them know the door is open: That is okay. Just know I am here whenever you want to talk, about anything.

Then keep in touch in normal ways. Invite them to things, send a message, and check in again later. Many people open up the second or third time someone asks.

If you are seriously worried about their safety, though, it is right to ask more directly. Later cards explain how.
cards.apply_it: If someone brushes you off, plan a simple way to check in again in a few days.

quiz.question: What should you do if someone says they are fine but you are still worried?
options: Never mention it again
Push until they admit something
Tell everyone you know
Let them know you are there and check in again later
quiz.explanation: Leaving the door open and checking in again shows care without pressure. People often open up later.

cards.title: Listen to understand, not to fix
cards.body:
When someone shares something painful, it is natural to want to fix it. But jumping to advice can make people feel unheard, as if their feelings are a problem to be solved quickly.

Often, what helps most is simply listening. Give them your full attention. Put your phone away. Let them talk at their own pace, and try not to interrupt.

Silence is okay. You do not need to fill every pause. Nodding, saying I see or that sounds really hard, shows you are with them.

If you are unsure whether they want ideas, you can ask: Would it help to think about what to do, or do you just need to talk for now?
cards.apply_it: In your next important conversation, put your phone away and focus only on listening.

quiz.question: Why can jumping straight to advice be unhelpful?
options: It can make people feel unheard
Advice is always wrong
Listening is less caring than advice
People never want any ideas
quiz.explanation: Rushing to fix things can leave people feeling unheard. Listening first helps them feel understood.

cards.title: Reflect back what you hear to show you understand
cards.body:
Reflecting means repeating back the heart of what someone has said, in a few words. It shows you are listening and helps them feel understood.

For example, if a friend says, I just cannot keep up at work and I feel like I am letting everyone down, you might say, It sounds like you are under a lot of pressure and worried about disappointing people.

You can also ask gentle open questions to understand more: What has that been like for you? What is the hardest part?

If you get it wrong, that is okay. They can correct you, and that still helps. The aim is to understand their experience, not to agree or disagree.
cards.apply_it: Next time someone shares a worry, reflect it back in one sentence before saying anything else.

quiz.question: Which response is an example of reflecting back?
options: You should just quit your job
Everyone feels like that
It sounds like you are under a lot of pressure and worried about letting people down
At least you have a job
quiz.explanation: Reflecting back sums up what the person said and felt, showing you have understood.

cards.title: Accept their feelings, even if you do not fully understand them
cards.body:
You do not have to understand exactly why someone feels the way they do to accept that the feelings are real. This is sometimes called validation.

Validating sounds like: That makes sense, given everything you are dealing with. Or: I can hear how painful this is for you. Or even: I do not fully understand, but I can see it is really hard, and I want to help.

Validation does not mean agreeing that things are hopeless or that their harshest thoughts about themselves are true. It means accepting their feelings without judgement.

People who feel accepted are more likely to keep talking and to accept help.
cards.apply_it: Practise one validating phrase you feel comfortable saying, such as I can see this is really hard.

quiz.question: What does validating someone's feelings mean?
options: Agreeing that things are hopeless
Telling them how they should feel
Fixing the problem for them
Accepting their feelings are real without judging them
quiz.explanation: Validation means accepting someone's feelings as real and understandable, without having to agree with every thought.

cards.title: Avoid phrases that play down what they feel
cards.body:
Some well-meant phrases can make people feel brushed off. Common ones include: Cheer up. It could be worse. Others have it harder. Just think positive. You have so much to be grateful for. It is all in your head.

These can suggest that the person should not feel the way they do, which may add guilt or shame and make them less likely to open up again.

Instead, try phrases that show you take them seriously: Thank you for telling me. That sounds really tough. I am here for you.

It is easy to slip into old phrases. If you notice you have, you can simply say, sorry, that came out wrong, I want to understand.
cards.apply_it: Pick one phrase you tend to say, like cheer up, and choose a kinder replacement.

quiz.question: Which phrase is most supportive?
options: Cheer up, it could be worse
Thank you for telling me, that sounds really tough
Others have it much harder
Just think positive
quiz.explanation: Phrases that play down feelings can add shame. Thanking them and acknowledging the difficulty shows you take them seriously.

cards.title: Avoid comparing, lecturing or making it about you
cards.body:
Other common traps are comparing, lecturing and turning the talk towards yourself.

Comparing sounds like: I felt like that once and I just got over it. Even if you mean to relate, it can sound as if their struggle is small or easy to fix.

Lecturing sounds like: You need to exercise more and stop drinking. Advice given too early or too firmly can feel like criticism.

Making it about you might be telling a long story of your own, or showing so much shock or upset that they end up comforting you.

It is fine to share a little of your experience if it helps them feel less alone. Just keep it short and bring the focus back to them.
cards.apply_it: In your next supportive chat, notice if you start to compare or lecture, and gently steer back to listening.

quiz.question: Why can comparing your own experience be unhelpful?
options: It always makes people feel better
It shows you are an expert
It can make their struggle seem small or easy to fix
It is a good way to end the conversation
quiz.explanation: Comparing can suggest their problem is small. A brief share is fine, but keep the focus on them.

cards.title: Asking directly about suicide is safe and can help
cards.body:
Many people fear that asking someone about suicide will put the idea in their head. Research shows this is not the case. Organisations including the NIMH, the NHS and the World Health Organization say that asking directly does not increase risk.

In fact, asking can bring relief. It shows you are willing to hear the hardest things and that the person does not have to carry them alone. It also gives you important information about how to help.

If you are worried about someone, it is better to ask clearly than to hint. Vague questions, like you are not going to do anything silly, are easy to brush off and can make people feel judged.
cards.apply_it: Remind yourself: asking about suicide does not put the idea in someone's head.

quiz.question: What does research say about asking someone directly about suicide?
options: Asking does not increase risk and can bring relief
It puts the idea in their head
You should only hint at it
Only doctors are allowed to ask
quiz.explanation: Research shows asking directly does not increase risk. It can help the person feel heard and open the way to help.

cards.title: Ask clearly and calmly, using the word suicide
cards.body:
If you are worried, it helps to ask in a clear, calm and caring way. You might say: Sometimes when people feel the way you do, they think about suicide. Are you having thoughts of suicide? Or more simply: Are you thinking about killing yourself?

Using clear words shows you are not afraid of the answer and that it is safe to be honest.

Try to stay calm whatever they say. Listen without judging, arguing or promising to keep it a secret.

It can feel scary to ask. That is normal. Many people find it helps to practise the words in advance, so they come out more easily when it matters.
cards.apply_it: Practise saying the question out loud on your own: Are you having thoughts of suicide?

quiz.question: Why is it better to use clear words like suicide when asking?
options: It is more dramatic
It means you can avoid listening
It is required by law
It shows you are not afraid of the answer and makes honesty easier
quiz.explanation: Clear, calm words show it is safe to talk honestly. Vague questions are easy to dodge.

cards.title: If they say yes, stay calm and stay with them
cards.body:
If the person says they are having thoughts of suicide, try to stay calm. Thank them for telling you. This took courage.

Listen and take what they say seriously. You can gently ask whether they have thought about how or when, and whether they feel they might act soon. This helps you understand how urgent things are.

If they are in immediate danger, or have a plan and the means to act, do not leave them alone. Contact local emergency services, a crisis line, or help them get to a hospital emergency department.

If the danger is not immediate, help them make contact with a doctor or crisis line soon, and agree when you will next check in.
cards.apply_it: Write down what you would do, step by step, if someone told you they were thinking of suicide.

quiz.question: If someone has a plan and is in immediate danger, what should you do?
options: Leave them to calm down alone
Stay with them and contact emergency services or a crisis line
Promise to keep it a secret
Tell them to sleep on it
quiz.explanation: In immediate danger, stay with them and get urgent help from emergency services, a crisis line or an emergency department.

cards.title: In a crisis, focus on safety and getting help fast
cards.body:
A mental health crisis is when someone is at immediate risk of harming themselves or others, or is too distressed to stay safe.

The NIMH suggests five action steps: ask, keep them safe, be there, help them connect, and follow up.

In practice: contact local emergency services or a crisis line. Stay with the person if it is safe for you to do so. If you can safely do it, help put distance between them and things they could use to harm themselves, such as medicines or sharp objects. Speak calmly and simply. Do not argue or lecture.

If you feel at risk yourself, move to safety and call emergency services. Your safety matters too.
cards.apply_it: Save the details of local emergency services and a crisis line in your phone now.

quiz.question: Which are the NIMH's five action steps?
options: Ignore, wait, hope, forget, move on
Fix, advise, lecture, decide, leave
Ask, keep them safe, be there, help them connect, follow up
Call, shout, argue, insist, report
quiz.explanation: The NIMH's steps are ask, keep them safe, be there, help them connect and follow up.

cards.title: A safety plan can help someone through dark moments
cards.body:
A safety plan is a short, written plan someone can use when suicidal thoughts or distress rise. It is often made with a professional, but you can help the person think it through.

It usually includes: warning signs that a crisis may be starting; things they can do to cope on their own, like going for a walk or listening to music; people and places that help distract them; people they can ask for help; professionals and crisis lines to contact; and ways to make their surroundings safer.

Keeping the plan on their phone or somewhere easy to find means it is there when thinking is hard.

A safety plan supports, but does not replace, professional care.
cards.apply_it: Look up a free safety plan template from a mental health charity, so you know what one looks like.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of a safety plan?
options: To give steps to follow when suicidal thoughts or distress rise
To replace all professional care
To keep secrets from doctors
To list their mistakes
quiz.explanation: A safety plan lists warning signs, coping steps and people to contact, so the person has a clear guide in hard moments.

cards.title: Encourage them to talk to a doctor or other professional
cards.body:
Friends and family are important, but many people also need professional help. A doctor is often a good first step. They can talk about options such as talking therapy or medication, and point to local services.

You could say: I think it might help to talk to a doctor. Would you like me to help you book an appointment?

Some people prefer to start with a counsellor, a helpline, or a support service at school, university or work. Many places also offer self-referral to talking therapy services.

If they are reluctant, try to understand why. They might worry about being judged, about medication, or about cost. Talking through these fears can help.
cards.apply_it: Find out how someone in your area can see a doctor or refer themselves for talking therapy.

quiz.question: What is a good way to encourage someone to get professional help?
options: Insist they go or you will stop talking to them
Book a doctor without telling them
Tell them therapy is for weak people
Gently suggest it and offer to help them book
quiz.explanation: A gentle suggestion with an offer of practical help makes it easier for someone to take the step.

cards.title: Practical help can make the first step easier
cards.body:
When someone is struggling, even small tasks can feel huge. Making a phone call or filling in a form might feel impossible.

You can offer practical help, such as finding phone numbers, helping them write down what they want to say, sitting with them while they call, or going with them to an appointment and waiting outside.

Ask what would help most, rather than taking over. For example: Would it help if I came with you, or would you prefer I check in afterwards?

After appointments, check how it went. If the first professional is not a good fit, encourage them to keep trying. Finding the right support can take time.
cards.apply_it: Offer one specific piece of practical help, such as going with someone to an appointment.

quiz.question: What is the best approach to practical help?
options: Take over and make all their decisions
Ask what would help most and offer specific support
Leave them to manage alone
Only help if they ask three times
quiz.explanation: Offering specific help while respecting their choices supports them without taking away their control.

cards.title: If they refuse help, stay connected and keep the door open
cards.body:
It can be frustrating and frightening when someone you love will not get help. But adults usually have the right to make their own choices, and pushing too hard can make them withdraw.

Keep showing that you care. Let them know you will support them whenever they are ready. Share information, like a website or helpline, without pressure. Sometimes people change their mind after time to think.

You can also get advice for yourself. Many mental health charities offer support for friends and family.

The exception is when there is an immediate risk to their life or someone else's. Then it is right to contact emergency services, even if they do not want you to.
cards.apply_it: Find one source of advice for family and friends that you could use if someone refuses help.

quiz.question: When is it right to get help even if the person does not want it?
options: Whenever they disagree with you
If they are a bit quiet
If there is an immediate risk to their life or others' safety
Never, under any circumstances
quiz.explanation: Adults usually choose for themselves, but if there is immediate danger to life, getting emergency help is the right step.

cards.title: Do not promise to keep a secret if their safety is at risk
cards.body:
Someone might say, I will tell you, but you have to promise not to tell anyone. It is natural to want to agree to keep their trust.

But if what they share puts them or someone else at risk, you may need to get help. It is kinder to be honest from the start. You could say: I will keep what you tell me private as much as I can, but if I am worried about your safety, I will need to get help.

Most people understand this. If you do need to tell someone, try to involve the person in the decision and explain why.

You are not betraying them by keeping them safe.
cards.apply_it: Practise saying: I will keep this private if I can, but not if your safety is at risk.

quiz.question: What should you say if someone asks you to keep a secret about their safety?
options: I promise never to tell anyone, whatever happens
I will tell everyone straight away
I do not want to know
I will keep it private if I can, but not if your safety is at risk
quiz.explanation: Being honest about the limits of secrecy protects their safety and your trust at the same time.

cards.title: Keep checking in, because support matters over time
cards.body:
Recovery from mental health problems often takes weeks or months, and there may be ups and downs. A single conversation is a great start, but ongoing contact matters.

The NIMH lists follow up as one of its key steps. Research suggests that simple, regular contact after a crisis can help reduce risk.

You do not need long, deep talks every time. A quick message, a cup of tea, or saying I was thinking of you, shows you are still there.

Try to keep in touch even if they do not always reply. People who are struggling may not have the energy to respond, but they often still notice and value the contact.
cards.apply_it: Set a reminder to check in with the person you are supporting once a week.

quiz.question: Why is ongoing contact important?
options: Recovery often takes time, and regular contact can help
One conversation is always enough
Checking in annoys everyone
Only professionals should stay in touch
quiz.explanation: Recovery takes time. Regular, simple contact shows you care and can help after a crisis.

cards.title: Everyday practical help can lighten a heavy load
cards.body:
When someone is struggling, daily life can pile up. Dishes, shopping, bills and emails can feel overwhelming, and this can make them feel even worse.

Practical help can be a real relief. You could drop off a meal, help with shopping, walk the dog, look after the children for an afternoon, or sit with them while they open their post.

Be specific when you offer. Can I bring dinner on Thursday? is easier to accept than let me know if you need anything, because people often feel bad asking.

Respect their wishes. Some people want help with tasks; others want to keep doing things themselves to feel in control.
cards.apply_it: Make one specific offer of practical help this week, such as bringing a meal on a set day.

quiz.question: Which offer is easiest for someone to accept?
options: Let me know if you need anything
Can I bring dinner on Thursday?
You should really clean up
I could help one day, maybe
quiz.explanation: Specific offers are easier to say yes to than vague ones, because people often feel uncomfortable asking.

cards.title: Treat them as the same person, not as a problem
cards.body:
When someone is struggling with their mental health, they are still the same person. They still have interests, humour and opinions. Being treated only as someone who is ill can feel lonely.

Keep inviting them to things, even if they often say no. Talk about everyday topics too, like football, films or family news, not just their feelings. Laugh together if the moment is right.

Ask what they want: Would you like to talk about how you are doing, or would you rather just have a normal chat today?

Keeping ordinary life going can give a sense of normality and hope, and reminds them they belong.
cards.apply_it: Invite the person you are supporting to an ordinary, low-pressure activity they used to enjoy.

quiz.question: Why is it helpful to keep treating someone normally?
options: It means you can ignore their feelings
It makes them feel worse
It shows they are still valued and belong
It is a way to avoid helping
quiz.explanation: Treating someone as the same person helps them feel valued and gives a sense of normal life and hope.

cards.title: Be patient, because recovery is rarely a straight line
cards.body:
It is natural to hope that once someone gets help, they will quickly feel better. But recovery often has ups and downs. There may be good weeks followed by hard ones.

Try not to show frustration or say things like you were doing so well. Setbacks are common and do not mean that all progress is lost.

Notice and gently point out small improvements: you seem to have a bit more energy this week. But avoid putting pressure on them to be better.

Respect their pace and their choices about treatment, even if you would do things differently. Your steady presence matters more than speed.
cards.apply_it: Write down one small positive change you have noticed in the person, and mention it kindly.

quiz.question: How should you respond to a setback in someone's recovery?
options: Say you were doing so well, what happened?
Assume all progress is lost
Stop supporting them
Stay patient and remind yourself setbacks are common
quiz.explanation: Ups and downs are normal in recovery. Patience and steady support help more than frustration.

cards.title: You can still support someone from a distance
cards.body:
Not everyone you care about lives nearby. You can still offer real support from far away.

Regular messages, calls and video chats help people feel less alone. Sending a card, a small gift or a photo can show you are thinking of them. Some friends watch a film at the same time and chat about it, or play an online game together.

If you are worried about their safety and they are far away, you can still help. Encourage them to contact local emergency services or a crisis line, or, if they are in immediate danger and you know where they are, contact the emergency services for their area yourself.

It can also help to know who else is near them, such as a family member or flatmate.
cards.apply_it: Schedule a regular call or video chat with someone you care about who lives far away.

quiz.question: If someone far away is in immediate danger, what can you do?
options: Contact the emergency services for their area if you know where they are
Nothing, distance means you cannot help
Wait until you can visit
Send a funny video and hope for the best
quiz.explanation: Even from far away, you can get emergency help to them if they are in immediate danger and you know their location.

cards.title: Supporting a young person means staying calm and involved
cards.body:
Teenagers and children can find it hard to explain their feelings. Changes like dropping grades, losing friends, staying in their room, being very irritable, or changes in sleep and eating can be signs they are struggling, as well as normal ups and downs.

Try to stay calm and curious, rather than angry or panicked. Make time for low-pressure chats, like in the car or while cooking. Listen more than you talk.

Let them know you love them no matter what. Talk to their school, and see a doctor if you are worried. For young people, it is especially important not to keep safety concerns secret.

If there is immediate danger, contact local emergency services.
cards.apply_it: Plan a low-pressure time to chat with a young person in your life, such as during a car ride.

quiz.question: What is a good way to support a struggling teenager?
options: Shout so they take it seriously
Stay calm, make time for low-pressure chats and seek help if worried
Ignore it as just a phase
Promise to keep every worry secret
quiz.explanation: Calm, regular chats and getting help from school or a doctor support young people best.

cards.title: Look after yourself so you can keep supporting others
cards.body:
Supporting someone who is struggling can be tiring and worrying. You might feel stressed, sad, guilty or even resentful at times. These feelings are normal.

Looking after yourself is not selfish. It is what lets you keep going. Keep doing things you enjoy, get enough sleep, eat well, and spend time with people who lift you up.

Set boundaries. You cannot be available every minute, and you are not responsible for fixing everything. It is okay to say, I can talk for half an hour tonight, but I need to sleep after that.

Remember that you are one part of their support, not all of it. Professionals and others can share the load.
cards.apply_it: Plan one thing this week that is just for you, such as a walk, a hobby or time with a friend.

quiz.question: Why is it important for supporters to set boundaries?
options: Because they should not care too much
Because the person should cope alone
So they can keep supporting without burning out
So they never have to listen
quiz.explanation: Boundaries protect your own wellbeing, which means you can keep offering support over time.

cards.title: Get support for yourself as a supporter
cards.body:
You do not have to carry worry alone. Talk to someone you trust about how you are feeling, while respecting the other person's privacy as much as you can.

Many mental health charities offer information and support groups for friends, family and carers. Talking with others in a similar situation can help you feel less alone and learn new ideas.

If supporting someone is affecting your own sleep, mood or health, talk to your own doctor. Supporters can become stressed, anxious or low too.

If you have been through a frightening event, like a crisis or a suicide attempt, you may feel shaken for some time afterwards. Getting support for yourself is important and normal.
cards.apply_it: Look up one support group or service for friends and family of people with mental health problems.

quiz.question: What should a supporter do if their own sleep or mood is suffering?
options: Ignore it and keep going
Stop all contact with the person
Hide it from everyone
Talk to their own doctor and seek support
quiz.explanation: Supporters can struggle too. Seeing a doctor and getting support are normal and important steps.

cards.title: Notice, ask, listen and help them connect to support
cards.body:
You can make a real difference to someone who is struggling. Notice lasting changes in what they do and say. Choose a calm moment and ask gently, with open questions, and ask twice if needed.

Listen to understand, reflect back what you hear, and accept their feelings. Avoid phrases that play down their pain.

If you are worried about suicide, ask directly and calmly. It is safe and can help. In a crisis, stay with them if it is safe and contact local emergency services or a crisis line straight away.

Encourage professional help, offer practical support, and keep checking in over time. And look after yourself too.
cards.apply_it: Choose one skill from this guide to practise this week, such as asking twice or reflecting back.

quiz.question: Which summary of this guide is most accurate?
options: Notice, ask, listen, help them find support, and look after yourself
Fix their problems quickly
Avoid talking about suicide at all costs
Leave support to professionals only
quiz.explanation: Noticing, asking, listening, helping them connect to support and caring for yourself are the key steps.
